claim: Cerebellar plasticity underlies motor learning.
source: Cerebellar plasticity underlies motor learning.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Before training, simple spikes of individual Purkinje cells correlated during reflexive protraction with the whisker position without lead or lag.
source: Before training, simple spikes of individual Purkinje cells correlated during reflexive protraction with the whisker position without lead or lag.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data on Purkinje cell recordings and whisker tracking.

claim: After training, simple spikes and whisker protractions were both enhanced with the spiking activity now leading behavioral responses.
source: After training, simple spikes and whisker protractions were both enhanced with the spiking activity now leading behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data comparing pre- and post-training conditions.

claim: Neuronal and behavioral changes did not occur in two cell-specific mouse models with impaired long-term potentiation at their parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses.
source: Neuronal and behavioral changes did not occur in two cell-specific mouse models with impaired long-term potentiation at their parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments using Pcp2-Ppp3r1 and Pcp2-Gria3 mutant mice.

claim: Increased simple spike activity was prominent in cells with low complex spike response probability.
source: Consistent with cerebellar plasticity rules, increased simple spike activity was prominent in cells with low complex spike response probability.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of Purkinje cell responses.

claim: Potentiation at parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses may contribute to reflex adaptation.
source: Thus, potentiation at parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses may contribute to reflex adaptation and enable expression of cerebellar learning through increases in simple spike activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and mutant mouse studies.

claim: Active touch is important for exploring our environment, allowing us to assess the shape, substance and movements of objects and organisms around us.
source: Active touch is important for exploring our environment, allowing us to assess the shape, substance and movements of objects and organisms around us (Prescott et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Various systems have evolved for active touch including the antennae of insects, the fingertips of primates and the well-developed whisker systems of rodents and sea mammals.
source: Throughout the animal kingdom, various systems have evolved for this purpose; these include for example the antennae of insects, the fingertips of primates and the well-developed whisker systems of rodents and sea mammals (Ahl, 1986; Dehnhardt et al., 2001; Staudacher et al., 2005; Dere et al., 2007; Anjum and Brecht, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of sensory organs can provoke reactive movements, often occurring as a reflex.
source: Activation of these sensory organs can provoke reactive movements, often occurring as a reflex (Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005; Bellavance et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018; Staudacher et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: It is important to maintain optimal control of reflexes in daily life and to be able to adapt these movements.
source: For survival, it is important to maintain optimal control of such reflexes in daily life and to be able to adapt these movements (Voigts et al., 2015; Anjum and Brecht, 2012; Arkley et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adaptation of reflexive whisker movements is partly controlled by plastic processes in the cerebellum.
source: Given the impact of cerebellar plasticity on a wide variety of motor learning tasks (Herzfeld et al., 2015; Herzfeld et al., 2018; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Thier et al., 2002; Voges et al., 2017; Yang and Lisberger, 2017), it can be anticipated that adaptation of reflexive whisker movements is also partly controlled by plastic processes in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Most studies on cerebellar learning have suggested that long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapse may act as the main cellular mechanism underlying induction of cerebellar motor learning.
source: Historically, most studies on cerebellar learning have suggested that long-term depression (LTD) at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell (PC) synapse may act as the main cellular mechanism underlying induction of cerebellar motor learning (Albus, 1971; Konnerth et al., 1992; Ito, 1989; Koekkoek et al., 2003; Medina and Lisberger, 2008; Boele et al., 2018; Narain et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior work supported by multiple citations.

claim: Parallel fiber LTD is unlikely to be the sole cellular mechanism underlying cerebellar learning.
source: However, parallel fiber LTD is unlikely to be the sole cellular mechanism underlying cerebellar learning (Gao et al., 2012; Hansel et al., 2001; D'Angelo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Short-term forms of plasticity probably also contribute to behavioral adaptation.
source: Short-term forms of plasticity probably also contribute, as some forms of behavioral adaptation can be linked to changes in PC activity during the previous trial (Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) of parallel fiber to PC synapses may be relevant for cerebellar learning.
source: Moreover, long-term potentiation (LTP) of parallel fiber to PC synapses may also be relevant, as various PC-specific mutants with impaired LTP show deficits in cerebellar learning (Schonewille et al., 2010; Schonewille et al., 2011; Rahmati et al., 2014; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Different cerebellar cellular mechanisms may dominate the induction of different forms of learning, dependent on the requirements of the downstream circuitries involved.
source: Possibly, different cerebellar cellular mechanisms dominate the induction of different forms of learning, dependent on the requirements of the downstream circuitries involved (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; Suvrathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The expression of conditioned eyeblink responses is mediated by a long-lasting suppression of simple spikes of PCs in the deep fissure of lobule simplex.
source: To date, whereas evidence is emerging that the expression of conditioned eyeblink responses is mediated by a long-lasting suppression of simple spikes of PCs in the deep fissure of lobule simplex (Heiney et al., 2014; Halverson et al., 2015; ten Brinke et al., 2015), it is unclear to what extent enduring increases in simple spike activity can also contribute to the expression of cerebellar learning, and if so for what forms of learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is unclear to what extent enduring increases in simple spike activity can contribute to the expression of cerebellar learning.
source: To date, whereas evidence is emerging that the expression of conditioned eyeblink responses is mediated by a long-lasting suppression of simple spikes of PCs in the deep fissure of lobule simplex (Heiney et al., 2014; Halverson et al., 2015; ten Brinke et al., 2015), it is unclear to what extent enduring increases in simple spike activity can also contribute to the expression of cerebellar learning, and if so for what forms of learning.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on prior work.

claim: A novel whisker training paradigm was developed that is likely to generate plasticity in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Here, we developed a novel whisker training paradigm that is likely to generate plasticity in the cerebellar cortex and to produce increases in simple spike activity at the PC level following induction of LTP at the parallel fiber to PC synapse (D'Angelo et al., 2001; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Coesmans et al., 2004; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016; van Beugen et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach developed in this study, with citations to prior work on LTP mechanisms.

claim: A brief period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation of the whiskers can enhance touch-induced whisker protraction.
source: Indeed, we show that a brief period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation of the whiskers can enhance touch-induced whisker protraction as well as PC simple spike firing for tens of minutes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: A brief period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation of the whiskers can enhance PC simple spike firing for tens of minutes.
source: Indeed, we show that a brief period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation of the whiskers can enhance touch-induced whisker protraction as well as PC simple spike firing for tens of minutes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Behavioral and neuronal changes are absent in two independent mouse mutant lines deficient for parallel fiber to PC LTP.
source: Moreover, these behavioral and neuronal changes are both absent in two independent mouse mutant lines deficient for parallel fiber to PC LTP, bridging the putative mechanism of memory expression with that of memory induction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments using mutant mice.

claim: Passive touch can trigger active whisker movements in mice.
source: It has been noted that passive touch can trigger active whisker movements in mice (Bellavance et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018; Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005; Ferezou et al., 2007), but this behavior has not been described in great detail yet.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mice made active whisker protractions following the retractions induced by the air flow in 82% of stimulus trials.
source: The mice made active whisker protractions following the retractions induced by the air flow in the large majority (82%) of stimulus trials (Figure 1D–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data.

claim: Touch-induced protraction was typically performed by all whiskers simultaneously.
source: Because of the systematic full-field air-flow from the front, the touch-induced protraction was typically performed by all whiskers simultaneously (data not shown), which is in line with the presumed reflexive nature of this movement (Bellavance et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018; Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by citations to prior work on reflexive movements.

claim: Touch-induced whisker protraction was followed in about half the trials (51%) by extended periods of active whisker movements during the subsequent 200 ms interval.
source: Moreover, as reported previously (Ferezou et al., 2007), the touch-induced whisker protraction was followed in about half the trials (51%) by extended periods of active whisker movements during the subsequent 200 ms interval (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data, with citation to prior work.

claim: Spontaneous whisking in between stimuli was relatively rare under the experimental conditions with a 2 s inter-trial interval.
source: However, under our experimental conditions with a 2 s inter-trial interval, spontaneous whisking in between the stimuli was relatively rare.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's experimental data.

claim: Spontaneous movements with an amplitude exceeding 10° were found only in 12% of the 100 trials per mouse during the 200 ms interval prior to stimulus onset.
source: Across all 16 mice measured, we found spontaneous movements (with an amplitude exceeding 10°) only in 12% of the 100 trials per mouse during the 200 ms interval prior to stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data.

claim: Applying the air-puff from different angles produced different retractions and different subsequent protractions.
source: Thus, applying the air-puff from different angles produced different retractions and different subsequent protractions, arguing against a stereotypical startle behavior that occurs independent from the stimulus conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments testing different stimulus conditions.

claim: No distinct explorative movements linked to the puff sources were observed.
source: Finally, we also did not observe distinct explorative movements linked to the puff sources, which might have suggested dominant voluntary components (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's behavioral data.

claim: The reactive nature of the touch-induced whisker movements in the absence of characteristic signs of startle or voluntary responses indicates that the air-puff induced protraction is a reflexive movement.
source: Altogether, the reactive nature of the touch-induced whisker movements in the absence of characteristic signs of startle or voluntary responses indicates that the air-puff induced protraction is indeed a reflexive movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: PCs receive sensory whisker input both directly from the brainstem and indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways.
source: In line with the fact that PCs receive sensory whisker input not only directly from the brainstem but also indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways (Figure 2F) (Kleinfeld et al., 1999; McElvain et al., 2018; Bosman et al., 2011; Brown and Raman, 2018; Kubo et al., 2018), the dynamics of their responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous (Brown and Bower, 2001; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The dynamics of PC responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous.
source: In line with the fact that PCs receive sensory whisker input not only directly from the brainstem but also indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways (Figure 2F) (Kleinfeld et al., 1999; McElvain et al., 2018; Bosman et al., 2011; Brown and Raman, 2018; Kubo et al., 2018), the dynamics of their responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous (Brown and Bower, 2001; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Of the 132 single-unit PCs recorded, 118 (89%) showed significant complex spike responses.
source: Of the 132 single-unit PCs from which we recorded, 118 (89%) showed significant complex spike responses, albeit with large variations in latency and amplitude (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claim: Cluster analysis revealed that in terms of complex spike modulation PCs can be considered as two separate clusters rather than a continuous spectrum.
source: Cluster analysis revealed that in terms of complex spike modulation PCs can better be considered as two separate clusters rather than a continuous spectrum (indicated by the lowest absolute BIC value for two components (437, compared to 490 and 442 for one and three components, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claim: 34% of PCs were classified as 'strong' complex spike responders and 66% as 'weak' responders.
source: We refer to the cells of the cluster with the higher complex spike response probability as 'strong' (34%, with a peak response above 1.98%; see Materials and methods) and the other as 'weak' (66%) responders (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from cluster analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claim: Of the 132 recorded PCs, 127 (96%) showed a significant simple spike response.
source: Similarly, of the 132 recorded PCs 127 (96%) showed a significant simple spike response.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claim: Simple spike responses were often bi-phasic, consisting of a period of inhibition followed by one of excitation, or vice versa.
source: Simple spike responses were often bi-phasic, consisting of a period of inhibition followed by one of excitation, or vice versa (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's electrophysiological data.

claim: The trough of the simple spike responses typically correlated in a reciprocal fashion with the peak of the complex spike responses.
source: The trough of the simple spike responses typically correlated in a reciprocal fashion with the peak of the complex spike responses (Figure 2A–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C) (De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014; Badura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiological data, with citations to prior work.

claim: Only 2 PCs out of 132 did not show any significant modulation for either complex spikes or simple spikes.
source: Only 2 PCs, out of the 132, did not show any significant modulation (i.e. for neither complex spikes nor simple spikes).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claim: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones.
source: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were found to be especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones (Figure 2H), whereas the primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2, as predicted by the overall tendency for reciprocity (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of electrophysiological responses.

claim: Primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2.
source: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were found to be especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones (Figure 2H), whereas the primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2, as predicted by the overall tendency for reciprocity (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of electrophysiological responses.

claim: PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1.
source: These experiments confirmed that the PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1, whereas the PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical tracing experiments.

claim: PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2.
source: These experiments confirmed that the PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1, whereas the PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical tracing experiments.

claim: Complex spikes have been reported to encode the destination of arm movements at the start of a movement.
source: As complex spikes have been reported to be able to encode, at the start of a movement, the destination of arm movements (Kitazawa et al., 1998), we wondered whether a similar association could be found for whisker movements.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During trials with a complex spike, the protraction was significantly larger than trials without a complex spike.
source: It turned out that during the trials with a complex spike, the protraction was significantly larger (see Figure 3A for a single PC; Figure 3B for the population of 55 PCs of which we had electrophysiological recordings during whisker tracking and that responded to air-puff stimulation).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the relationship between complex spikes and whisker movements.

claim: The peak in complex spike activity preceded the moment of maximal difference in position by 63 ± 4 ms.
source: A direct comparison between the timing of the complex spike response and the difference in whisker position between trials with and without a complex spike revealed that the peak in complex spike activity preceded the moment of maximal difference in position by 63 ± 4 ms (mean ±SEM; n = 55; Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The maximal difference in protraction in trials with a complex spike equaled 0.80° (median, with IQR of 2.80°; p<0.001).
source: The maximal difference in protraction in trials with a complex spike equaled 0.80° (median, with IQR of 2.80°; p<0.001), whereas this was only 0.28° (0.92°) for retraction (p=0.002; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons: α = 0.05/3 = 0.017) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Trials that started with a complex spike showed bigger whisker protractions than those without a complex spike.
source: These findings imply that trials that started with a complex spike showed bigger whisker protractions than those without a complex spike.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There was no obvious correlation between the strength of the complex spike response of any given PC and the difference in touch-induced whisker protraction in trials with and without a complex spike.
source: This did not seem to be the case (R = 0.119; p=0.386; Pearson correlation; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of the data.

claim: The complex spike of any PC showing whisker-related complex spike activity could have a similar predictive power for the amplitude of the subsequent protraction.
source: Thus, in general, the complex spike of any PC showing whisker-related complex spike activity could have a similar predictive power for the amplitude of the subsequent protraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: Complex firing in the D2 zone had the strongest predictive value for increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
source: Thus, complex firing in the D2 zone had the strongest predictive value for increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of PC responses.

claim: Motor control can be related to the coherence of complex spike firing of adjacent PCs.
source: Previous studies showed that motor control can be related to the coherence of complex spike firing of adjacent PCs (Mukamel et al., 2009; Hoogland et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon whisker pad stimulation, complex spike firing occurred much more often collectively in multiple PCs.
source: Upon whisker pad stimulation, however, complex spike firing occurred much more often collectively in multiple PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from two-photon calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The levels of coherence increased to such strength that they were extremely unlikely to have occurred by the increase in firing frequency alone.
source: The levels of coherence increased to such strength that they were extremely unlikely to have occurred by the increase in firing frequency alone (compared to a re-distribution of all events based on a Poisson distribution; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the imaging data.

claim: Firing of a single or a few PCs was the dominant mode of activity in the absence of stimulation, and this changed toward the involvement of multiple PCs upon stimulation, firing coherently.
source: In other words, firing of a single or a few PCs was the dominant mode of activity in the absence of stimulation, and this changed toward the involvement of multiple PCs upon stimulation, firing coherently as can be seen in the change in distribution of coherently active PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the imaging data.

claim: Groups of adjacent PCs respond to whisker pad stimulation by increased complex spike firing with an enhanced level of coherence.
source: We conclude that groups of adjacent PCs respond to whisker pad stimulation by increased complex spike firing with an enhanced level of coherence, which is likely to further facilitate the occurrence of bigger whisker reflexes (see above).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data.

claim: In the large majority of PCs, simple spike firing is correlated with protraction and in a minority it correlates with retraction.
source: The firing rate of simple spikes has been shown to correlate with whisker position: in the large majority of PCs, simple spike firing is correlated with protraction and in a minority it correlates with retraction (Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In 25 of the 56 PCs (45%), there was a positive correlation between instantaneous simple spike firing and whisker protraction that occurred relatively late during the movement, in particular between 80 and 200 ms after the start of the stimulus.
source: This turned out to be the general pattern in 25 of the 56 PCs (45%) of which we had electrophysiological recordings during whisker tracking (Figure 4D). In all these 25 PCs, there was a positive correlation between instantaneous simple spike firing and whisker protraction that occurred relatively late during the movement, in particular between 80 and 200 ms after the start of the stimulus (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), thus well after the complex spike responses occurred (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis of the data.

claim: In the 31 remaining PCs that did not display a significant correlation at the individual cell level, a slight yet significant negative correlation was observed at the population level.
source: In the 31 remaining PCs, that is the ones that did not display a significant correlation when evaluated at the level of individual cells, we still observed a slight, yet significant, correlation at the population level. Remarkably, this correlation was slightly negative, that is possibly reflecting a correlation between simple spike firing and retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from population-level correlation analysis.

claim: During the touch-induced whisker reflex simple spikes predominantly correlate with whisker protraction and this correlation is maximal without a clear time lead or lag.
source: We conclude that during the touch-induced whisker reflex simple spikes predominantly correlate with whisker protraction and that this correlation is maximal without a clear time lead or lag, unlike the complex spikes, the occurrence of which tended to precede the reflexive protraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses in reduced preparations.
source: We hypothesized that whisker movements might be enhanced following air-puff stimulation at 4 Hz, as this frequency has been shown to be particularly effective in inducing potentiation at the parallel fiber-to-PC synapse (Coesmans et al., 2004; D'Angelo et al., 2001; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Application of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation to the whisker pad for only 20 s was sufficient to induce an increase in the maximal protraction (average increase 17.9 ± 3.9%; mean ±SEM; p<0.001; Wilcoxon-matched pairs test; n = 16 mice).
source: Indeed, application of this 4 Hz air-puff stimulation to the whisker pad for only 20 s was sufficient to induce an increase in the maximal protraction (average increase 17.9 ± 3.9%; mean ±SEM; p<0.001; Wilcoxon-matched pairs test; n = 16 mice) (Figure 5A–B; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the training experiments.

claim: The change in the amplitude of the touch-induced whisker protraction was not accompanied by any substantial change in the complex spike response to whisker pad stimulation (p=0.163; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs).
source: This change in the amplitude of the touch-induced whisker protraction was not accompanied by any substantial change in the complex spike response to whisker pad stimulation (p=0.163; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claim: The rate of simple spike firing upon air-puff stimulation was markedly increased after 20 s of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, especially during the first 60 ms after the air-puff (p=0.003; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs).
source: However, the rate of simple spike firing upon air-puff stimulation was markedly increased after 20 s of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation. This was especially clear during the first 60 ms after the air-puff (p=0.003; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claim: The short period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation caused an anticipation of the moment of maximal correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position.
source: The short period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation caused an anticipation of the moment of maximal correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position. Along the 45° line – thus regarding only the zero-lag correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position – this changed from 152.1 ± 18.1 ms to 90.7 ± 9.4 ms (means ± SEM); p=0.020; t = 2.664; df = 13; paired t test; n = 14 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis.

claim: The slope of the correlation between the instantaneous simple spike frequency and the whisker position remained unaltered after 4 Hz stimulation (p=0.197, t = 1.360, df = 13, n = 14, paired t test).
source: The slope of the correlation between the instantaneous simple spike frequency and the whisker position remained unaltered (p=0.197, t = 1.360, df = 13, n = 14, paired t test) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claim: After induction, the simple spikes led the whisker position (pre-induction: Δtime = 0 ± 10 ms; post-induction: Δtime = 20 ± 30 ms; medians ± IQR; n = 14; p=0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
source: However, the point of maximal correlation was no longer with a zero-lag, but after induction the simple spikes led the whisker position (pre-induction: Δtime = 0 ± 10 ms; post-induction: Δtime = 20 ± 30 ms; medians ± IQR; n = 14; p=0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis.

claim: Not only the simple spike rate increased, but also its relative timing to the touch-induced whisker protraction changed, now preceding the likewise increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
source: Thus, not only the simple spike rate increased, but also its relative timing to the touch-induced whisker protraction changed, now preceding the likewise increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis.

claim: During the entrainment itself, the whisker responses as well as the complex spike and the simple spike responses to each air-puff were weakened compared to the pre-induction period.
source: During the entrainment itself (i.e. during the 20 s period with 4 Hz air-puff stimulation), the whisker responses as well as the complex spike and the simple spike responses to each air-puff were weakened compared to the pre-induction period during which we used 0.5 Hz stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of responses during different stimulation frequencies.

claim: The touch-induced whisker protraction decreased by 62.2% (median; IQR = 37.5%) during 4 Hz stimulation.
source: More specifically, the touch-induced whisker protraction decreased by 62.2% (median; IQR = 37.5%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data.

claim: The maximum response of the complex spikes significantly decreased from a median of 1.27% (with an IQR of 1.89%) during pre-induction to 0.52% (with an IQR of 0.43%) during induction (p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, n = 55 PCs).
source: The maximum response of the complex spikes significantly decreased from a median of 1.27% (with an IQR of 1.89%) during pre-induction to 0.52% (with an IQR of 0.43%) during induction (p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, n = 55 PCs), and the average modulation of the simple spikes in the first 200 ms after the puff decreased from a median of 5.9% (with an IQR of 18.2%) during pre-induction to -0.3% (IQR = 3.13) during induction (p=0.039, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claim: During the 4 Hz training stage, all responses – both at the behavioral and neuronal level – diminished compared to the preceding 0.5 Hz stimulation stage.
source: Thus, during the 4 Hz training stage, all responses – both at the behavioral and neuronal level – diminished compared to the preceding 0.5 Hz stimulation stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of responses during different stimulation frequencies.

claim: Contralateral air-puff stimulation triggers a stronger protraction than ipsilateral stimulation.
source: Given the correlation between instantaneous simple spike rate and whisker position described above, one would expect that contralateral air-puff stimulation – which triggers a stronger protraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) – also triggers a stronger simple spike response.
evidence: This is a finding from experiments comparing ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation.

claim: The change in maximal protraction between contralateral and ipsilateral stimulation was considerable (difference in maximal protraction: 7.30 ± 1.24° (mean ±SEM); n = 9 mice).
source: The change in maximal protraction was considerable (difference in maximal protraction: 7.30 ± 1.24° (mean ±SEM); n = 9 mice) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C; cf. Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison experiments.

claim: The simple spikes increased significantly more during contralateral stimulation (increase during first 60 ms after air-puff onset for contra- vs. ipsilateral stimulation: 13.7 ± 5.3%; mean ±SEM; p=0.023; t = 2.413; df = 26; paired t test; n = 27 PCs).
source: However, in addition a change in simple spikes may contribute to this difference as well, as the simple spikes increased significantly more during contralateral stimulation (increase during first 60 ms after air-puff onset for contra- vs. ipsilateral stimulation: 13.7 ± 5.3%; mean ±SEM; p=0.023; t = 2.413; df = 26; paired t test; n = 27 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the comparison data.

claim: The complex spikes were less activated during contralateral stimulation (complex spike peak response: ipsilateral: 1.40% (1.25%); contralateral: 0.71% (0.81%); medians (IQR); p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test; n = 27 PCs).
source: Instead, the complex spikes were less activated during contralateral stimulation (complex spike peak response: ipsilateral: 1.40% (1.25%); contralateral: 0.71% (0.81%); medians (IQR); p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test; n = 27 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the comparison data.

claim: Simple spikes modulate ongoing whisker movements rather than initiate them.
source: Previously, it has been shown that simple spikes modulate ongoing whisker movements rather than initiate them (Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016; Proville et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The whisker protraction was substantially bigger during the period of optogenetic stimulation (p<0.001; t = 4.411; df = 12; paired t test; n = 13 mice).
source: As expected, the whisker protraction was substantially bigger during the period of optogenetic stimulation (p<0.001; t = 4.411; df = 12; paired t test; n = 13 mice; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from optogenetic experiments.

claim: Increases in simple spike firing can cause stronger whisker protraction.
source: Thus, even though optogenetic stimulation of PCs can also trigger secondary feedback mechanisms that may influence the outcome (Witter et al., 2013; Chaumont et al., 2013), we conclude that increases in simple spike firing can cause stronger whisker protraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments, with citations to prior work on potential confounds.

claim: Cerebellar plasticity is bi-directional and under control of climbing fiber activity.
source: As cerebellar plasticity is bi-directional and under control of climbing fiber activity (Ohtsuki et al., 2009; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Coesmans et al., 2004), we wanted to find out to what extent plastic changes in simple spike activity can be related to the strength of the complex spike response generated by climbing fibers.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between the strength of the complex spike response before 4 Hz air-puff stimulation and the change in simple spike response following this 4 Hz stimulation (R = 0.311; p=0.021; Pearson correlation; n = 55 PCs).
source: As expected, we found a significant negative correlation between the strength of the complex spike response, as measured by the peak of the PSTH before the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, and the change in simple spike response following this 4 Hz stimulation (R = 0.311; p=0.021; Pearson correlation; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The correlation between the frequency of complex spike firing and the change in simple spike activity after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation was present only in the weak responders.
source: The correlation found between the frequency of complex spike firing and the change in simple spike activity after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation proved to be present only in the weak responders, taking the firing rate during the pre-induction and induction period into account (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from subgroup analysis of the correlation data.

claim: Parallel fiber activity in the absence of climbing fiber activity promotes parallel fiber to PC LTP.
source: This is again in line with the notion that parallel fiber activity in the absence of climbing fiber activity promotes parallel fiber to PC LTP (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The PCs with the strongest effect of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on simple spike firing were mainly located in the lateral part of crus 2.
source: The PCs with the strongest effect of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on simple spike firing were mainly located in the lateral part of crus 2 (Figure 6B), posterior to the crus 1 area with the strongest complex spike responses (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of the plasticity effects.

claim: The lateral crus 2 area with the strongest simple spike increase matched well with the area showing the strongest correlations between simple spike firing and whisker protraction.
source: We compared the location of this lateral crus 2 area to that of the PCs with the strongest correlations between simple spike firing and whisker protraction and we found these two crus 2 locations to match well (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of anatomical maps.

claim: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the simple spike activity of PCs with a weak complex spike response lasted at least 30 min.
source: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the simple spike activity of PCs with a weak complex spike response lasted as long as our recordings lasted (i.e. at least 30 min), whereas that on PCs with a strong complex spike response was not detectable during this period (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is a finding from long-term recording of PC activity.

claim: The weak responders differed significantly from the strong responders in the duration of simple spike changes (weak vs. strong responders: p=0.005; F = 3.961; df = 4.424; two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 weak and n = 6 strong responders).
source: Indeed, the weak responders differed significantly from the strong responders in this respect (weak vs. strong responders: p=0.005; F = 3.961; df = 4.424; two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 weak and n = 6 strong responders; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis comparing subgroups.

claim: The impact of the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction also lasted throughout the recording.
source: Likewise, the impact of the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction also lasted throughout the recording in that the protraction sustained (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from long-term behavioral measurements.

claim: Both simple spikes and whisker muscles remained affected by the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation for as long as the recordings lasted.
source: Thus, both simple spikes and whisker muscles remained affected by the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation for as long as our recordings lasted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the long-term recording data.

claim: In reduced preparations, 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses.
source: In reduced preparations, 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Parallel fiber LTP is inhibited by climbing fiber activity.
source: At the same time, parallel fiber LTP is inhibited by climbing fiber activity (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Ohtsuki et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The data appear in line with a role for parallel fiber LTP as a potential mechanism underlying the observed increase in simple spike firing upon a brief period of 4 Hz stimulation.
source: Hence, our data appear in line with a role for parallel fiber LTP as a potential mechanism underlying the observed increase in simple spike firing upon a brief period of 4 Hz stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data and prior knowledge.

claim: Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice lack the PP2B protein specifically in their PCs, rendering them deficient of parallel fiber-to-PC LTP.
source: To further test a potential role for LTP, we repeated our 4 Hz air-puff stimulation experiments in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice, which lack the PP2B protein specifically in their PCs, rendering them deficient of parallel fiber-to-PC LTP (Schonewille et al., 2010) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This describes the genetic model used, with citation to prior work.

claim: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the maximal protraction was significantly less in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mutant mice compared to wild types (p=0.044, t = 2.162, df = 19, t test).
source: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the maximal protraction was significantly less in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mutant mice compared to wild types (p=0.044, t = 2.162, df = 19, t test; Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparison of mutant and wild-type mice.

claim: In wild-type littermates, the maximal touch-induced whisker protraction before and after induction was significantly different (p<0.001, t = 4.122, df = 15, t test).
source: Accordingly, in contrast to those in their wild-type (WT) littermates (p<0.001, t = 4.122, df = 15, t test), the maximal touch-induced whisker protraction before and after induction was not significantly different in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (p=0.647, t = 0.470, df = 12, t test; Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: In Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice, the maximal touch-induced whisker protraction before and after induction was not significantly different (p=0.647, t = 0.470, df = 12, t test).
source: Accordingly, in contrast to those in their wild-type (WT) littermates (p<0.001, t = 4.122, df = 15, t test), the maximal touch-induced whisker protraction before and after induction was not significantly different in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (p=0.647, t = 0.470, df = 12, t test; Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice do not show increased touch-induced whisker protraction after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation.
source: Thus, Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice do not show increased touch-induced whisker protraction after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant mouse experiments.

claim: The increase in simple spike firing observed in wild type mice was absent in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice.
source: In line with the absence of increased touch-induced whisker protraction, also the increase in simple spike firing observed in wild type mice was absent in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of mutant and wild-type mice.

claim: Simple spike responses were stably increased in WT PCs with a weak complex spike response following 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, but not in those of Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (effect of genotype: p=0.003, F = 4.361, df = 4.137, two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 WT and n = 9 Pcp2-Ppp3r1 PCs).
source: Simple spike responses were stably increased in WT PCs with a weak complex spike response following 4 Hz air-puff stimulation (as shown in Figure 6F), but not in those of Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (effect of genotype: p=0.003, F = 4.361, df = 4.137, two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 WT and n = 9 Pcp2-Ppp3r1 PCs) (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical comparison of genotypes.

claim: Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice still had a significant correlation between the complex spike frequency during the induction block and changes in simple spike activity (R = 0.489, p=0.013, Pearson correlation).
source: Despite the lack of potentiation, we found that the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice still had a significant correlation between the complex spike frequency during the induction block and changes in simple spike activity (R = 0.489, p=0.013, Pearson correlation; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A); this correlation may result from other forms of plasticity that are still intact in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (Schonewille et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the mutant mice, with citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of the PP2B protein in PCs, the impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction as well as on the simple spike responsiveness was not detectable.
source: Thus, in the absence of the PP2B protein in PCs, the impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction as well as on the simple spike responsiveness was not detectable.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant mouse experiments.

claim: The correlations between complex spike and simple spike firing and modification of the simple spike response to whisker pad stimulation strengthen the hypothesis that parallel fiber to PC LTP is one of the main mechanisms underlying the long-term changes.
source: These correlations between complex spike and simple spike firing on the one hand and modification of the simple spike response to whisker pad stimulation on the other hand further strengthen our hypothesis that parallel fiber to PC LTP is one of the main mechanisms that underlies the long-term changes that can be observed at both the level of simple spike activity and whisker protraction after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses and mutant experiments.

claim: Pcp2-Gria3 mice lack the AMPA receptor GluA3 subunit specifically in their PCs.
source: In these mice (Pcp2-Gria3), PCs lack the AMPA receptor GluA3 subunit (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the genetic model used, with citation to prior work.

claim: No evidence for increased whisker protraction after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation was found in Pcp2-Gria3 mice (change in whisker angle during the first 120 ms after air-puff onset: WT vs. Pcp2-Gria3 mice: p=0.007, Tukey's post-hoc test after ANOVA (p=0.001, F = 9.111, df = 2), n = 16 WT and n = 6 Gria3 deficient mice).
source: As in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice, we did not find evidence for increased whisker protraction after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation (e.g., change in whisker angle during the first 120 ms after air-puff onset: WT vs. Pcp2-Gria3 mice: p=0.007, Tukey's post-hoc test after ANOVA (p=0.001, F = 9.111, df = 2), n = 16 WT and n = 6 Gria3 deficient mice) (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical comparison of genotypes.

claim: The increase in simple spike responsiveness after 4 Hz stimulation was absent in Pcp2-Gria3 mice (difference in simple spike count between WT and Pcp2-Gria3 PCs during the first 60 ms after air-puff onset: p=0.004; Tukey's post-hoc test after ANOVA (p=0.002, F = 6.681, df = 2), n = 35 WT PCs and n = 13 Gria3 KO PCs, next to n = 23 Pcp2-Ppp3r1 KO PCs, all with weak complex spike responses).
source: Moreover, as in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice, also the increase in simple spike responsiveness after 4 Hz stimulation was absent in Pcp2-Gria3 mice (difference in simple spike count between WT and Pcp2-Gria3 PCs during the first 60 ms after air-puff onset: p=0.004; Tukey's post-hoc test after ANOVA (p=0.002, F = 6.681, df = 2), n = 35 WT PCs and n = 13 Gria3 KO PCs, next to n = 23 Pcp2-Ppp3r1 KO PCs, all with weak complex spike responses) (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical comparison of genotypes.

claim: An independent line of evidence supports the findings made in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice.
source: Thus an independent line of evidence supports the findings made in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Pcp2-Gria3 experiments.

claim: Compared to their WT littermates, Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice had a mildly reduced complex spike rate.
source: When averaged over the entire period with episodes of stimulation, the overall complex spike rate, simple spike rate and simple spike CV2 value (i.e. parameter for level of irregularity) of PCs in the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 KO mice were moderately, but significantly, reduced compared to those in WTs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of baseline electrophysiological properties.

claim: Pcp2-Gria3 mice did not show any significant deviations in overall firing properties compared to wild types.
source: However, as the Pcp2-Gria3 mice did not show any significant deviations in these overall firing properties (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D; Supplementary file 1C), it is unlikely that the aberrant firing properties of Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice could explain the lack of adaptation at both the behavioral and electrophysiological level.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of baseline electrophysiological properties.

claim: Both the number of complex spikes and simple spikes after the air-puff were reduced in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice.
source: Comparing the response probabilities to whisker pad stimulation we found that both the number of complex spikes and simple spikes after the air-puff were reduced in Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–J; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of sensory responses.

claim: The predominantly suppressive simple spike responses were not found in Pcp2-Gria3 mice, but the latter also had a reduced complex spike response to air-puff stimulation.
source: The predominantly suppressive simple spike responses were not found in Pcp2-Gria3 mice, but the latter also had a reduced complex spike response to air-puff stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of sensory responses.

claim: The amplitudes of the touch-induced whisker protraction as measured before the induction phase were similar between the WT and the mutant mice.
source: Moreover, the amplitudes of the touch-induced whisker protraction as measured before the induction phase were similar between the WT and the mutant mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of baseline behavioral responses.

claim: The absence of simple spike potentiation and the concomitant increase in touch-induced whisker protraction is likely due to the absence of parallel fiber LTP caused by the genetic mutations rather than to altered firing patterns of the PCs involved.
source: We therefore conclude that the absence of simple spike potentiation and the concomitant increase in touch-induced whisker protraction is likely due to the absence of parallel fiber LTP caused by the genetic mutations rather than to altered firing patterns of the PCs involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant mouse experiments.

claim: A brief period of intense sensory stimulation can evoke adaptation of reflexive whisker protraction.
source: In this study, we show for the first time that a brief period of intense sensory stimulation can evoke adaptation of reflexive whisker protraction.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: The simple spike activity of the PCs that modulate during whisker movements is congruently increased when the adapted behavior is expressed.
source: Extracellular recordings revealed that the simple spike activity of the PCs that modulate during whisker movements is congruently increased when the adapted behavior is expressed.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: PCs that are predominantly located in the crus 2 region show a present but weak complex spike response to whisker stimulation, which appears to act permissive for the occurrence of parallel fiber to PC LTP.
source: These PCs, which are predominantly located in the crus 2 region, show a present but weak complex spike response to whisker stimulation, which appears to act permissive for the occurrence of parallel fiber to PC LTP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and electrophysiological data.

claim: Parallel fiber to PC LTP is likely to be one of the main mechanisms underlying whisker reflex adaptation.
source: This form of plasticity is likely to be one of the main mechanisms underlying this whisker reflex adaptation, as two independent cell-specific mouse models, both of which lack LTP induction at their parallel fiber to PC synapses, did not show any alteration in their whisker protraction or simple spike response following the training protocol with 4 Hz air-puff stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant mouse experiments.

claim: PCs that show a strong complex spike response to whisker stimulation and that are mainly located in crus 1 did not manifest a prominent regulatory role to enhance the simple spike responses or whisker movements in the long-term.
source: By contrast, the PCs that show a strong complex spike response to whisker stimulation and that are mainly located in crus 1 did not manifest a prominent regulatory role to enhance the simple spike responses or whisker movements in the long-term.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and electrophysiological data.

claim: Moderate climbing fiber activity may permit induction of PC LTP in a behaviorally relevant context.
source: Our study highlights how moderate climbing fiber activity may permit induction of PC LTP in a behaviorally relevant context and how this induction may lead to an increase in simple spike modulation when the adapted motor output is expressed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In 'whisking' animals, such as mice and rats, both whisker protraction and retraction are under direct muscle control.
source: In 'whisking' animals, such as mice and rats, both whisker protraction and retraction are under direct muscle control, while especially whisker retraction can additionally reflect a passive process involving skin elasticity (Berg and Kleinfeld, 2003; Simony et al., 2010; Haidarliu et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2013; Deschênes et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Animals can modify the pattern of whisker movements upon sensory feedback during natural behavior.
source: Animals can modify the pattern of whisker movements upon sensory feedback during natural behavior, as has been demonstrated for example during gap crossing and prey capture (Anjum and Brecht, 2012; Voigts et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The neural control of adaptation of reflexive whisker movements is still largely unknown.
source: The neural control of adaptation of reflexive whisker movements is still largely unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: For a specific reproducible form of whisker adaptation, parallel fiber to PC LTP and enhancement in PC simple spike activity may contribute to the induction and expression of motor learning, respectively.
source: We show here, at least for a specific reproducible form of whisker adaptation, that parallel fiber to PC LTP and enhancement in PC simple spike activity may contribute to the induction and expression of this form of motor learning, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Under the baseline condition, simple spikes correlate positively with the position of the whiskers during protraction on a single-trial basis.
source: Under the baseline condition of our paradigm, during the 0.5 Hz whisker pad stimulation, simple spikes correlate positively with the position of the whiskers during protraction on a single-trial basis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claim: The absence of a clear time lag or lead between simple spike activity and whisker movements under baseline conditions suggests that during normal motor performance without sensorimotor mismatch signaling the simple spikes predominantly represent ongoing movement.
source: The absence of a clear time lag or lead between simple spike activity and whisker movements under this condition suggests that during normal motor performance without sensorimotor mismatch signaling the simple spikes predominantly represent ongoing movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal correlation data.

claim: The simple spike activity of most PCs in the lateral crus 1 and/or crus 2 regions correlated best with protraction of the set point, defined as the slowly varying midpoint between maximal protraction and maximal retraction.
source: In their studies on online motor performance, the simple spike activity of most PCs in the lateral crus 1 and/or crus 2 regions correlated best with protraction of the set point, defined as the slowly varying midpoint between maximal protraction and maximal retraction.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from prior work by other labs.

claim: During and after training with 4 Hz air-puff stimulation the temporal dynamics of the simple spikes shifted in that the simple spikes were found to precede the whisker movement and to predict the magnitude of the protraction.
source: During and after training with 4 Hz air-puff stimulation the temporal dynamics of the simple spikes shifted in that the simple spikes were found to precede the whisker movement and to predict the magnitude of the protraction, suggesting the emergence of an instructive motor signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's training experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation experiments confirmed that increased simple spike firing during the early phase of touch-induced whisker protraction can promote whisker protraction.
source: Optogenetic stimulation experiments confirmed that increased simple spike firing during the early phase of touch-induced whisker protraction can promote whisker protraction.
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The current dataset confirms and expands on previous studies, highlighting a role of the cerebellar PCs injecting additional accelerating and amplifying signals into the cerebellar nuclei during entrainment.
source: Thus, the current dataset confirms and expands on previous studies, highlighting a role of the cerebellar PCs injecting additional accelerating and amplifying signals into the cerebellar nuclei during entrainment (De Zeeuw et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, with citation to prior work.

claim: Synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex has been recognized as one of the major mechanisms underlying motor learning.
source: Synaptic plasticity in the cerebellar cortex has, next to that in the cerebellar and vestibular nuclei (Lisberger and Miles, 1980; Lisberger, 1998; Zhang and Linden, 2006; McElvain et al., 2010), generally been recognized as one of the major mechanisms underlying motor learning (Ito, 2001; Ito, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For forms of motor learning that require a decrease in simple spike activity for expression of the memory, such as eyeblink conditioning, long-term depression (LTD) of the parallel fiber to PC synapse may play a role during the initial induction stage.
source: For forms of motor learning that require a decrease in simple spike activity for expression of the memory, such as eyeblink conditioning (Halverson et al., 2015; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Jirenhed et al., 2007), long-term depression (LTD) of the parallel fiber to PC synapse may play a role during the initial induction stage (Ito, 1989; Koekkoek et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In LTD-deficient mouse models the potential contribution of LTD is most apparent when compensatory mechanisms that involve activation of the molecular layer interneurons are blocked.
source: In LTD-deficient mouse models the potential contribution of LTD is most apparent when compensatory mechanisms that involve activation of the molecular layer interneurons are blocked (Boele et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: For forms of motor learning that require an increase in simple spike activity for expression of the procedural memory it is less clear which forms of cerebellar cortical plasticity may contribute.
source: However, for forms of motor learning that require an increase in simple spike activity for expression of the procedural memory it is less clear which forms of cerebellar cortical plasticity may contribute.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Increasing whisker protraction by repetitive sensory stimulation requires an increase in simple spike activity.
source: Here, we show that increasing whisker protraction by repetitive sensory stimulation requires an increase in simple spike activity and that blocking induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP prevents changes in both spiking and motor activity following the same training paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Blocking induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP prevents changes in both spiking and motor activity following the training paradigm.
source: Here, we show that increasing whisker protraction by repetitive sensory stimulation requires an increase in simple spike activity and that blocking induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP prevents changes in both spiking and motor activity following the same training paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutant mouse experiments.

claim: Adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) may follow partly similar learning rules in that various genetic mouse models with impaired induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP show reduced VOR learning.
source: Possibly, adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) follows partly similar learning rules in that various genetic mouse models with impaired induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP show reduced VOR learning (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017; Rahmati et al., 2014; Schonewille et al., 2010; Ly et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2016) and that optogenetic stimulation of PCs in the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum can increase VOR gain (Voges et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PCs in the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum can increase VOR gain.
source: Possibly, adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) follows partly similar learning rules in that various genetic mouse models with impaired induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP show reduced VOR learning (Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017; Rahmati et al., 2014; Schonewille et al., 2010; Ly et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2016) and that optogenetic stimulation of PCs in the flocculus of the vestibulocerebellum can increase VOR gain (Voges et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Different forms of cerebellar plasticity may dominate the induction of different forms of learning.
source: The differential learning rules highlighted above indicate that different forms of cerebellar plasticity may dominate the induction of different forms of learning (Hansel et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2012; D'Angelo et al., 2016; De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The engagement of different plasticity rules may depend on the requirements of the downstream circuitries involved.
source: The engagement of these rules may depend on the requirements of the downstream circuitries involved (Suvrathan et al., 2016; De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The eyeblink circuitry downstream of the cerebellar nuclei comprises purely excitatory connections and hence requires a simple spike suppression of the inhibitory PCs to mediate closure of the eyelids.
source: Indeed, whereas the eyeblink circuitry downstream of the cerebellar nuclei comprises purely excitatory connections and hence requires a simple spike suppression of the inhibitory PCs to mediate closure of the eyelids, the VOR circuitry comprises an additional inhibitory connection and hence requires a simple spike enhancement so as to increase the compensatory eye movement (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; Voges et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The VOR circuitry comprises an additional inhibitory connection and hence requires a simple spike enhancement so as to increase the compensatory eye movement.
source: Indeed, whereas the eyeblink circuitry downstream of the cerebellar nuclei comprises purely excitatory connections and hence requires a simple spike suppression of the inhibitory PCs to mediate closure of the eyelids, the VOR circuitry comprises an additional inhibitory connection and hence requires a simple spike enhancement so as to increase the compensatory eye movement (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; Voges et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The circuitry downstream of the cerebellum that mediates control of whisker movements is complex.
source: The circuitry downstream of the cerebellum that mediates control of whisker movements is complex (Bosman et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The cerebellar nuclei may modulate the trigemino-facial feedback loop in the brainstem that controls the touch-induced whisker protraction.
source: Possibly, the cerebellar nuclei may modulate the trigemino-facial feedback loop in the brainstem that controls the touch-induced whisker protraction (Bellavance et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior work.

claim: The cerebellar nuclei could modulate the trigemino-facial feedback loop via the intermediate reticular formation, which receives a direct input from the cerebellar nuclei and projects to the facial nucleus where the whisker motor neurons reside.
source: This could be done via the intermediate reticular formation, which receives a direct input from the cerebellar nuclei (Teune et al., 2000) and projects to the facial nucleus where the whisker motor neurons reside (Zerari-Mailly et al., 2001; Herfst and Brecht, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior work on anatomical connections.

claim: The projection from the reticular formation to the facial nucleus is inhibitory.
source: As the latter projection is inhibitory (Deschênes et al., 2016), the same configuration may hold as described for the VOR pathways (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015) in that adaptive enhancement of the whisker reflex may require induction of parallel fiber to PC LTP and increases in simple spike activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.
